opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think synthetic data is going to be one of the big levers over the next few years, and the way I think about priorities is basically: where is the bottleneck? For a long time the bottleneck was compute and architecture. We've made a lot of progress there, and now it feels like data quality and coverage is becoming the constraint. We've scraped most of the high-quality text on the internet, so the question is how you keep improving the models.

I'd put the top priority on domains where you can verify the output. Math, code, anything with a checker or a unit test or a simulator. If you can generate a lot of candidate solutions and automatically tell which ones are correct, then synthetic data becomes really powerful. You're not just recycling what the model already knows; you're filtering for things that are actually right, and that gives you a real signal to learn from. That's a big part of why reasoning models got so much better so quickly.

The second priority is targeting the gaps. Instead of generating huge amounts of generic data, you look at where the model is weak, like long-context reasoning, specific tool use, or rare domains, and you generate data specifically for those. It's much more efficient than just scaling up the pretraining mix.

Where I'm more cautious is open-ended domains where there's no clear verifier. There you risk the model training on its own mistakes and its own stylistic quirks, and you can get this kind of collapse in diversity. So you need a lot of care with filtering, mixing in real data, and making sure you're not just amplifying what's already there.

From my side, coming from the systems and efficiency angle, one thing I find exciting is that inference is now a big part of the training pipeline. If you're generating billions of tokens of synthetic data, the cost and speed of inference really matters. So a lot of the work we do on making inference faster and cheaper directly feeds into how much synthetic data you can afford to generate and how good you can make it. In a sense, efficiency work and data work are becoming the same problem.

r001.rationale: The response says inference speed and cost matter for generating large volumes, but does not prioritize throughput over latency.

r002.rationale: It discusses generating synthetic data and filtering it, but does not describe using a small amount of expert or human-annotated data to produce a much larger dataset.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss models simulating human customer personas.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about it on a couple of axes. The first is just: where is the data bottleneck actually binding? For a lot of the pretraining-scale stuff, we've basically run through most of the high-quality text on the internet, so the question becomes whether you can use a model to generate more tokens that actually carry new information, versus just restating what the model already knows. And that distinction matters a lot. If you sample from a model and train on its own outputs, you're mostly just distilling the model into itself, and you can get this collapse where the distribution narrows and you lose the tails. So the naive version of "generate more data" doesn't buy you much.

Where I think synthetic data is genuinely powerful is when you have some verifier or some source of signal that isn't the model itself. Code is the obvious example: you generate a program, you run it, you have tests, you know whether it's right. Math is similar if you have a checker or a formal system. In those domains the model is really acting as a proposal distribution, and the environment is doing the filtering, and that's where you can get something like actual new information into the training set. So priority one for me is: pair generation with verification wherever you can.

The second axis is what you're trying to teach. For a lot of post-training, you don't need the data to contain new facts about the world; you need it to shape behavior. Formatting, following instructions, reasoning step by step, knowing when to say "I don't know." There, synthetic data is great because you can control the distribution very precisely. You can target the exact failure modes you see and generate thousands of examples around them, which you'd never get from scraping.

And then the third thing, which people underweight, is cost. Generating a trillion tokens with a big model is not free. So you end up caring a lot about the efficiency of the generator, both in the sense of inference throughput and in the sense of how many samples you need to get one good one after filtering. That's actually one of the places where the systems work and the data work meet. If you can make inference 3x cheaper, that directly translates into either more synthetic data or a bigger, better model doing the generating. So I don't really see "synthetic data" as a separate research direction from efficiency; they feed each other pretty directly.

r001.rationale: The response mentions inference throughput as one part of generation efficiency, but does not prioritize it over latency or discuss large-batch generation.

r002.rationale: It discusses generating targeted synthetic examples but does not describe using a small set of expert or human-annotated data to create a much larger dataset.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention models simulating customer personas.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what capability are you trying to improve, and what data are you missing? It’s easy to generate a lot of text, but the volume by itself isn’t necessarily useful. You want examples that teach the model something it doesn’t already do well.

I’d prioritize settings where you can check the output. With code, for example, you can run tests. With some math problems, you can verify the answer. That gives you a way to select useful examples instead of just trusting whatever the generating model says. And then diversity matters—you don’t want a million variations of essentially the same easy problem.

Ultimately, I’d make it an experimental loop: generate a batch, train on it, and measure whether it improves performance on held-out tasks. The thing to optimize is the improvement you get from the data, rather than how much data you can produce.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes useful, verifiable data and measuring model improvement; it does not prioritize throughput over latency.

r002.rationale: It discusses generating batches of examples but does not describe using a small expert- or human-annotated dataset to create a larger synthetic dataset.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention models simulating human customer personas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what are you trying to improve with that data? If the model already does something well, generating another million examples of the same thing might not help very much. I’d start with the capabilities where it’s struggling and ask whether we can generate useful examples there.

Then verification becomes really important. For something like code, you can run the program and check whether it passes tests. That gives you a stronger signal than just asking the model whether its own answer looks good. Generating a lot of text is relatively easy; knowing which of it is useful is the harder part.

And I’d prioritize diversity and iteration. Generate some data, train on it, and measure whether it actually improves the capability you care about. That feedback loop matters more than the raw number of synthetic tokens.

r001.rationale: It discusses generating large amounts of data and measuring results, but does not prioritize throughput over latency for large-batch generation.

r002.rationale: It does not describe starting with expert or human-annotated examples and expanding them into a much larger synthetic dataset.

r003.rationale: It does not mention models simulating human customer personas.
